group: Unit iv — Risk Assessment & Operational Safety
title: Risk Mitigation, Safety Barriers & Preventive Measures

questions.q: The hierarchy of controls, in order of strength, is:
options: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) → Administrative → Engineering → Substitution → Elimination
questions.explain: Learn this order exactly as examiners ask it: remove it, replace it, engineer it, administer it, and only lastly wear protection against it.

questions.q: The strongest control in the hierarchy is:
questions.explain: No hazard, no risk. Elimination beats every control that merely manages the hazard.

questions.q: The weakest control, used as the last line, is:
options: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) — helmets, gloves, hi-vis
questions.explain: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) depends on the person wearing it correctly every time — that is why it ranks last.

questions.q: Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) having no level crossings is an example of:
options: Elimination — the hazard is removed by design
questions.explain: Designing out the train–road conflict removes the hazard completely instead of managing it daily.

questions.q: Replacing a risky manual process with an automated one is:
questions.explain: Substitution swaps the dangerous way of working for a safer one.

questions.q: Automatic Train Protection (ATP), interlocking and Platform Screen Doors are examples of:
questions.explain: Engineering controls build safety into the equipment itself — they work even when a human errs.

questions.q: Rules, permits, training, rostering and signage are:
questions.explain: Administrative controls organise human behaviour — strong, but they depend on people following them.

questions.q: Fire detection systems in a station are which type of control?
questions.explain: Detection is built into the system — an engineering layer that warns before humans notice.

questions.q: Why is Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) ranked below administrative controls?
options: Because it only protects if the individual wears it correctly every single time
questions.explain: Every higher control protects everyone automatically; Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) protects one person, only when worn right.

questions.q: A safety poster and a warning sign are best classified as:
questions.explain: Signs and posters try to guide behaviour — they do not physically prevent harm.

questions.q: A permit-to-work system is which type of control?
questions.explain: Permit to Work (PTW) organises who may work, where and when — a procedural barrier, vital but paper-based.

questions.q: Defence in depth means:
options: No single barrier is trusted alone — several different layers protect together
questions.explain: Design + Automatic Train Protection (ATP) + procedures + competent people + supervision + emergency preparedness: layers, not luck.

questions.q: In the Swiss-cheese model, an accident happens when:
options: The holes in several defensive layers line up at the same moment
questions.explain: Each layer has weaknesses; only when they align can the accident pass through all of them.

questions.q: Which is a physical barrier?
options: Platform Screen Doors and track fencing
questions.explain: Physical barriers physically prevent entry to the danger zone.

questions.q: Which is a functional barrier?
questions.explain: Functional barriers work through the system: Automatic Train Protection (ATP) stops the train, interlocking prevents conflicting routes.

questions.q: Which is a procedural barrier?
questions.explain: Procedural barriers live in how work is authorised and communicated.

questions.q: Which is a human barrier?
questions.explain: Competent, supervised people are themselves a layer of defence.

questions.q: Fail-safe design contributes to safety barriers by:
options: Making the system fall to a safe state when something fails
questions.explain: Fail-safe means a failure creates safety, not danger — signals fall to danger, not to green.

questions.q: Scenario: For a hazard, you can either issue helmets or redesign the layout to remove the hazard. The hierarchy says:
options: Redesign to eliminate the hazard — elimination outranks Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)
Do both equally; order does not matter
questions.explain: When a stronger control is reasonably practicable, choosing the weakest one is the wrong answer.

questions.q: Scenario: A manual trackside task is replaced by a remote/automated system. This control is:
questions.explain: Swapping a risky manual process for an automated one is the book's own substitution example.

questions.q: Closing a level crossing entirely is which control?
questions.explain: The book's elimination example: close the level crossing and the train–road hazard ceases to exist.

questions.q: Which set contains ONLY engineering controls?
options: Automatic Train Protection (ATP), interlocking, Platform Screen Doors (PSDs), fire detection
questions.explain: Engineering = built into equipment and infrastructure; the others guide people or protect individuals.

questions.q: Why do examiners stress the ORDER of the hierarchy?
options: Only Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) order matters
Because controls must be chosen from the strongest reasonably practicable level, not the most convenient
questions.explain: The hierarchy is a choosing rule: start at the top and justify any step down.

questions.q: A barrier that fails silently is dangerous mainly because:
options: Other layers may be trusted on the assumption that it is still working
questions.explain: Defence in depth assumes layers are alive; a silently dead layer leaves a hidden hole in the cheese.

questions.q: What is the role of emergency preparedness in the barrier system?
options: It is the final layer — limiting harm when all preventive barriers have failed
questions.explain: Prevention first, but preparedness catches what prevention misses — that is why it completes the layers.

questions.q: Supervision acts as a barrier by:
options: Catching errors and unsafe acts before they combine with other failures
questions.explain: A supervisor's verification is a human layer that plugs holes in the procedural layer.

questions.q: Scenario: A station fits Platform Screen Doors (PSDs) (engineering) AND trains staff in crowd control (administrative) AND posts signage. This is:
options: Defence in depth — different barrier types layered together
questions.explain: Layering different control types is exactly the intent — no single barrier is trusted alone.

questions.q: Which control would you choose FIRST for passengers falling from a platform edge?
options: An engineering control such as Platform Screen Doors (PSDs), supported by administrative measures like yellow-line discipline
questions.explain: Start high in the hierarchy: physically separate passengers from the edge, then support with rules and markings.

questions.q: Interlocking prevents accidents by:
options: Making it impossible to set conflicting routes — a functional/engineering barrier
questions.explain: Interlocking removes the human possibility of a conflicting route — the system itself refuses.

questions.q: A 'barrier' in operational safety is:
options: Any measure — physical, functional, procedural or human — that prevents a hazard causing harm or limits its effect
questions.explain: Barriers come in four families, and a safe railway stacks all four.

questions.q: Why is 'training' not an engineering control?
options: Training is not a control at all
Because it works through people's behaviour, not through the equipment
questions.explain: Training is administrative/human — valuable, but it depends on the person remembering and applying it.

questions.q: Scenario: After fitting Automatic Train Protection (ATP) (engineering), a railway removes all rules and training. Is safety improved overall?
options: No — removing layers weakens defence in depth; barriers are added, not traded away
questions.explain: A new barrier strengthens the stack; it is never a licence to strip other layers away.

questions.q: The Swiss-cheese model teaches managers to:
options: Add and maintain several different layers, and repair holes found in any layer
questions.explain: Holes are normal; the defence is numbers and variety of layers, plus fixing known holes.

questions.q: Which is the correct strength order among these three?
questions.explain: Built-in protection beats behaviour rules, which beat personal equipment — every time.

questions.q: Preventive measures differ from emergency preparedness in that they:
options: Act before an incident to stop it happening, rather than limiting harm after it starts
questions.explain: Prevention and preparedness are both needed, but they work on opposite sides of the incident.

questions.q: Safety barriers such as emergency braking and fire detection are proof-tested at planned intervals mainly because:
options: Testing is a formality for records
A barrier can fail silently (a dormant failure) and be unavailable on the one day it is demanded — testing reveals the hidden failure in time
Tests increase the speed of trains
questions.explain: Barriers that act only in emergencies spend their lives waiting — and can quietly die while waiting. Proof tests are demands made on purpose, so a dead barrier is found in the depot, not during a real emergency.

questions.q: Which of these is a PASSIVE safety barrier?
options: A sprinkler system that must detect heat and then discharge
A fire-resistant wall / fire door that simply exists and blocks fire spread without needing to act
A fire alarm that must sense and sound
An emergency fan that must start on command
questions.explain: Passive barriers work by merely being there — walls, doors, separation distances, fencing. Active barriers must detect, decide and act, so they have more ways to fail and need testing and power.

questions.q: Two safety barriers that both depend on the same power supply or the same single person are weaker than they appear because:
options: They are not truly independent — one common failure can defeat both barriers together (common-cause failure)
questions.explain: Layers only multiply safety when they fail independently. A shared power supply, shared sensor or shared person is a hidden thread joining the holes in the cheese slices — one failure can line them all up.

questions.q: In Safety Integrity Level (SIL) terms, a HIGHER SIL number (for example SIL 4 in signalling) means:
options: The safety function must fail far less often on demand — it is held to a much stricter reliability target
More staff are needed to operate it
questions.explain: Safety Integrity Level (SIL) grades how trustworthy a safety function must be. SIL 4, used for the most critical signalling functions, demands an extremely low probability of failure on demand — because when it is demanded, lives depend on it working.

questions.q: Why is preventive maintenance itself treated as part of the safety-barrier system?
options: Engineered barriers degrade with wear, dust and age — maintenance and inspection are what keep a barrier capable of performing when demanded
It is required for warranty only
questions.explain: A barrier on paper is not a barrier in reality. A Platform Screen Door (PSD) sensor blinded by dust or a brake valve overdue for overhaul is a hole already open in the slice — maintenance is what keeps designed protection real.
